note.question: When will competing auditors voluntarily adopt an interoperable permissioned blockchain, and when must a regulator coordinate or subsidize adoption to reduce misreporting and audit costs?
note.overview: Clients strategically choose misstatement probabilities and auditors choose monitoring intensities, fees, and blockchain adoption while competing for clients. The paper derives unique reporting-auditing and fee equilibria plus no-, partial-, and full-adoption equilibria and studies when a regulator can coordinate a welfare-improving outcome.

components.label: Model sequence and system structure
components.explanation: At the adoption stage, each auditor decides whether to incur the fixed cost of joining the federated blockchain. Conditional on the technology configuration, auditors post fees and clients choose auditors using audit quality, fee, and Hotelling fit. Once matched, each client chooses a misstatement probability while its auditor chooses a sampling intensity. The endogenous-partner extension adds an ex ante client choice of the private/off-chain transaction share before client type is known.

components.label: Backward-induction reporting-auditing, fee-competition, and federated-blockchain adoption equilibria
components.explanation: The model's equilibrium concept is Backward-induction reporting-auditing, fee-competition, and federated-blockchain adoption equilibria. Backward induction first gives a unique client-misstatement/auditor-monitoring equilibrium and then a unique interior fee-and-market-share equilibrium. Adding auditors' adoption choices produces parameter regions with unique no adoption, unique full adoption, or one/two partial-adoption equilibria. Because an adopting auditor can gain market share, partial adoption embodies a first-mover advantage; the private and social full-adoption thresholds need not coincide.
